resources.string: VBA macros
Visual Basic code stored in the document. Run by Word, Excel or PowerPoint, it can download and start programs, change files and read data. It is the most common way malicious documents attack.
Macro that runs by itself
A macro is set to start the moment the document is opened or closed, without any click. This is how most macro malware starts.
Excel 4.0 macro sheet
An old macro format that keeps commands in spreadsheet cells. Antivirus programs often miss it, and attackers use it to start programs.
Excel 4.0 macro that starts on opening
A special name (Auto_Open) makes an Excel 4.0 macro sheet run as soon as the workbook is opened.
LibreOffice Basic macros
Scripts in the Basic language of LibreOffice and OpenOffice stored in the document. They can run commands on the computer.
Embedded script
Python, JavaScript or BeanShell code stored in the document that an office program can run.
DDE field
A field that asks the system to run a command through Dynamic Data Exchange. It starts programs without any macro and is a well-known attack technique.
DDE formula in a cell
A spreadsheet cell holds a formula that calls another program through DDE. It can launch a command when the workbook is opened.
Dangerous formula
A spreadsheet formula that calls external programs, reads files or fetches data from the network (CALL, EXEC, WEBSERVICE and similar).
Embedded OLE object
An object of another program stored inside the document. When activated, the program that owns it is started, and such programs have many known vulnerabilities.
Packaged file
A file stored inside the document that Office can extract and run when you double-click its icon. A classic way to deliver a program.
Object of a type used in attacks
The object belongs to a component that has been used in real attacks (Equation Editor or MSHTML, for example). Opening it in Office could run the attacker’s code.
ActiveX control
A Windows control embedded in the document. Controls are programs and can do whatever the user can.
Custom toolbar with code
The document changes the program’s toolbar and attaches code to its buttons.
Action that starts a program
A button or shape in the document is wired to start a program or macro when it is clicked or pointed at.
MacroButton field
A Word field that runs a macro when it is clicked or when the document opens.
JavaScript in the PDF
A script inside the PDF. Readers that run PDF scripts can be attacked through them, and scripts can send data away or open other files.
PDF starts a program
The PDF asks the reader to start a program or open a file on the computer. This is almost never legitimate.
PDF action on opening
The PDF has an action that runs automatically when the document or a page is opened.
File inside the PDF
A file is attached inside the PDF. The reader can offer to extract it, and the attachment may be a program.
Active media in the PDF
The PDF contains Flash, 3D or other rich media that needs a plug-in with a long history of vulnerabilities.
Object inside the RTF
The RTF stores an embedded object. Word starts the program that owns it, and RTF objects have been used in many attacks.
RTF object that updates itself
The RTF object is set to refresh automatically on opening, so its program starts without a click.
Program inside the document
An executable file (EXE, DLL, script) is stored inside the document. A document has no honest reason to contain one.
Document inside the document
Another document is stored inside this one. It can carry its own macros, so it is inspected separately.
Script bound to an event
An OpenDocument file attaches a script to an event such as opening the document or clicking an element.
Digitally signed macros
The macros carry a signature. A signature only says who signed; it does not make the code safe, and stolen certificates are used in attacks. Arca does not trust it.
Active content in HTML
The page contains scripts, frames or event handlers that a browser would run.
Spreadsheet formula in a text table
A cell starts with =, +, - or @, so a spreadsheet program would treat it as a formula and could run commands. Arca shows it as plain text.
Imported external content
Word is told to pull in the content of another file when the document opens, which can bring in HTML or RTF with its own risks.
Template loaded from the internet
The document is set to download its template from a server when opened. Attackers use this to load malicious macros or to learn that the document was opened.
Picture loaded from the internet
A picture is fetched from a server when the document is opened. The server learns your address and the time, and can tell that the document was read.
Frame loaded from the internet
A frame displays content from a remote address that can change at any time.
Object linked to a remote address
An object is linked to a file or a server and is refreshed from there.
Link to another workbook
The workbook pulls data from another file or server. The address can reveal your network or load data you did not expect.
Data connection
The workbook connects to a database or web service when refreshed. It can send data out as well as bring data in.
Field that includes remote content
A field (INCLUDETEXT, INCLUDEPICTURE, LINK) fetches content from another address when the document is updated.
Network path (UNC)
The document refers to a Windows network path (it starts with two backslashes). Opening it makes Windows try to log in to that server, which can leak a password hash.
Link with a dangerous protocol
A link uses a protocol that starts programs or scripts (such as ms-msdt, file, javascript or vbscript).
Link to the internet
The document has a link to a web address. Arca never follows it.
Remote style sheet
The XML refers to an external style sheet, which can transform the content or fetch data.
Mail merge data source
The document is connected to a data file or database for mail merge, which makes Word open that connection.
PDF contacts a remote address
The PDF is set to open a web address or to submit a form to a server.
External resource
The document refers to something outside itself that is loaded when it is opened.
Base address for links
The document sets a base address that changes where its relative links lead.
Hidden sheet
A sheet that is not shown in the workbook’s tab bar. It may hold data, formulas or macros.
Very hidden sheet
A sheet that cannot be unhidden from the normal menu; only a macro or an editor can show it. There is almost always a reason to hide it this way.
Hidden rows or columns
Rows or columns exist but are not displayed.
Hidden text
Text is marked as hidden, so it neither shows nor prints, but it remains in the file.
Invisible text
Text is made invisible by a tiny size or by the same colour as the background.
Hidden slide
A slide that is skipped in the presentation but is still in the file.
Leftover data in the file
Parts that nothing refers to remain in the old-format file. They may be remains of earlier content or a hidden payload.
Unused files in the container
The container holds files that nothing in the document uses, which can hide data.
File that is two formats at once
The file can be read as two different formats, a trick used to get past checks.
Data after the end of the file
Extra bytes follow the real end of the file. Programs ignore them, and attackers hide payloads there.
Document variables
Word stores named values in the file. Macros can read them, so they are used to hide code or settings.
Custom XML data
Other programs have attached hidden data blocks to the document.
Preview picture of the document
A saved thumbnail may show an older version of the content, including text that was later deleted.
Text direction trick
Invisible characters reverse the order of text, for example to make a file name look like it ends in .txt when it ends in .exe.
Disguised name
A name in the document is written with random characters or tricks that hide what it really is.
Author information
The file carries the names of the people who created or changed it.
Path on the author’s computer
A folder path of the author’s machine is stored in the file, and it often contains a user name.
Printer information
The file stores the name of the printer that was used. It can reveal an office or a network.
Tracked changes
The file keeps the history of edits, including deleted text and who made the changes.
Comments
Reviewers’ notes are stored in the file.
Identifier tied to a person or device
The file contains identifiers (GUIDs, machine or account names) that can link it to its author.
Editing session identifiers
Word’s hidden revision-session numbers can show how and when the file was edited and can link files to each other.
Custom properties
Extra properties added by the author or by a program, sometimes with internal names or classification labels.
Damaged container
The internal structure of the file is broken or contradicts itself. Different programs may handle it differently, which attackers exploit.
Unusual compression
The archive uses a compression setting that honest programs do not produce.
Macro-enabled file type
The file is of a type built to carry macros (such as DOCM or XLSM).
Macros do not match the file type
The file says it has no macros but contains a macro project, or the other way round. Mislabelled files are used to slip past filters.
Program disguised as a document
The file is a program but has the name or icon of a document.
Unsupported format
Arca could not recognise the format, so it cannot vouch for the file.
Inspection limit reached
The file is so large or so deeply nested that the inspection stopped at its safety limit. The rest was not examined.
Embedded font
A font is stored in the file. Fonts are read by complex code that has been attacked before.
Decompression bomb
A small file that expands to a huge size, made to exhaust memory. It was stopped.
Path traversal in the archive
A file in the archive has a name such as ../ meant to escape its folder and overwrite other files when unpacked.
Inconsistent archive structure

The internal tables of the file disagree with each other (duplicate names, overlapping entries, mismatched headers), so different programs would read different content. Attackers use this to evade scanners.
XML entity attack
The XML is built so that reading it expands into a huge amount of data or fetches a local or remote file.
Encrypted document
The content is encrypted, so it cannot be examined. Encrypted attachments are often used to slip past scanners.
Encrypted part
A part inside the file is encrypted and could not be examined.
Camera, owner or serial number
The file names the camera or program, and sometimes its owner or serial number, which can identify who took the picture.
Embedded small copy
A small copy of the picture is stored inside it. Editing programs often leave the original, uncropped picture in it.
Photo records where it was taken
The file stores the GPS position of the place where the picture was taken. Anyone you send it to can see it.
Frames that are never shown
The picture has several frames (an animation). Only the first is shown; the others are not decoded.
Hidden metadata
The file carries extra metadata (a comment, an XMP packet, text chunks, a maker note or a colour profile). None of it is shown.
Picture too large to open safely
The picture declares a size so large that opening it could exhaust the memory of the device. It is not opened.
